full_text:
**Verdict: KNOWN-VARIANT, leaning toward KNOWN.** The behaviour itself is documented. What hasn't been written up is this exact pairing of mechanisms, and that alone isn't a discovery.

**1. The cyclic step is a known, named rule.** Rule (2) with 3 types, the 8-cell neighbourhood and threshold 3 is Griffeath's "313" rule. The MCell rule list gives it as R1/T3/C3/NM and calls it "the only three-color rule in the range-1 CCA rulespace that exhibits significant self-organization." It belongs to the threshold–range cyclic automaton family, where a cell's color advances by 1 if there are at least Threshold cells of the next color in its neighbourhood. That family's phases are mapped out. At intermediate thresholds incoherent traveling waves form, propagate, collide and disperse (the "turbulent" phase). For larger neighbourhoods, a complex mix of color blocks and partial spirals, called turbulence, can form.

**2. Adding a random copying or swapping step is also covered.** Rule (1) is a voter-model step; the SWAP siblings are an exchange step. Both work like mobility in rock-paper-scissors models. In those models, a critical threshold of motility is identified, above which biodiversity is lost, but below which an entanglement of travelling spiral waves emerges. The authors say this is robust, it does not depend on the details of cyclic competition or spatial environment. The stochastic, continuous-time version of cyclic competition is Bramson & Griffeath's cyclic particle system. The deterministic automaton was proposed by Bramson and Griffeath as the deterministic counterpart of the cyclic particle system. So this hybrid sits between two well-studied relatives.

**3. Why the fingerprint isn't textbook.** A correlation length of about 4.7 cells on a 64×64 grid, a few domains, balanced types (entropy ≈ 1) and a high reversal rate (0.5) look like strongly noise-disrupted cyclic waves. Copying a random neighbour every step with p=1 is heavy noise, so cells near domain borders flip back and forth. That likely explains most of the high reversal score; it's probably not new dynamics. My reading is that this sits in the known "turbulent / noisy cyclic domains" regime, with the noise keeping spiral cores small and short-lived. I found nothing in the behaviour that the literature leaves unexplained. The only gap is that no paper simulates exactly 313 plus every-step synchronous voter copying.

**Genuine or artifact?** The cyclic wave activity is genuine: it passes the standard test, and the deterministic 313 core is known to self-organise. The odd parts of the fingerprint (small domains, high reversals) are best read as what the noise step does to known dynamics, not a new pattern. 45 rule programs landing in the same class is what you'd expect if they all share a cyclic step plus a mixing step.

**How to make this KNOWN outright:** run 313 with no copy step on the same 64×64 grid with the same metrics, then turn the copy probability down gradually. If you see a smooth crossover from spirals to small turbulent domains, this is the standard noise-versus-spiral-size trade-off.
